newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe aims to reform constitution to help women.
newsitem.headline: Juppe aims to reform constitution to help women.

text.p: Prime Minister Alain Juppe wants to reform the constitution to help lift the number of women in French politics from the lowest in the 15-nation European Union, a member of his ruling coalition said on Tuesday.

Gilles de Robien, National Assembly floor leader for the centrist Union for French Democracy (UDF), told reporters that conservative Juppe would announce the plans during a debate in parliament later on Tuesday.

Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure declined to confirm the plan but said after a cabinet meeting the prime minister "is determined to go as far as possible in a dossier to which he gives priority".

Juppe came to office in May 1995 trumpeting a record 12 women in his cabinet, 30 percent of all ministers. But he sacked eight of them in a reshuffle later in the year, cutting their percentage to an unexceptional 13 percent.

In the National Assembly, women have only 32 seats out of 577, or 5.5 percent of the total, the worst record in the EU behind Greece and Britain. Women have most clout in Sweden, with 40 percent of seats.

De Robien said Juppe had hosted talks about women in politics at his office on Monday, after which he said that he would create a bill to reform the constitution to allow a better balanced participation in the national assembly.
"He will announce it this afternoon at the start of the debate," de Robien said, giving no details of the reform. The debate starts at 1500 GMT.
The opposition Socialist party has named women to 30 percent of the seats it will contest in National Assembly elections next year.

Some politicians favour writing the idea of parity into the constitution. Many in the government ranks argue such an amendment is unnecessary, saying that equality is one of the founding values of the French Revolution.
